prompt: What problem does Helm solve that plain YAML per environment does not?
answer_markdown: Raw manifests copied per environment drift apart. You start with three near-identical directories for dev, staging and prod, then a security fix gets applied to two of them, a memory limit gets bumped in prod only, and six months later nobody can state what differs between staging and prod — at which point "it works in staging" stops carrying information. Templating collapses that into one definition plus small per-environment value files. The manifest structure exists exactly once, so a change to it reaches every environment automatically, and what genuinely varies is explicit, small and reviewable in a single diff. The value is single-sourcing the structure, not saving keystrokes.

prompt: What is the difference between helm template and helm install, and why is rendering first considered the single most useful Helm habit?
answer_markdown: Both run the identical rendering pipeline — merge values, execute templates, produce YAML. Only install then applies the result to the cluster. Rendering first and actually reading the output is valuable because Helm performs text substitution and the result is parsed as YAML afterwards, so an entire class of bugs is invisible in the template and obvious in the output: a conditional that silently evaluated false, an empty block leaving structurally invalid YAML, a value that rendered as the string "nil", a block injected at the wrong indentation column. Reasoning about what a template should produce is unreliable; looking at what it does produce takes seconds. For an upgrade to an existing release, the diff plugin is the version of this you actually want, since it shows the change against what is currently deployed rather than the full manifest.

prompt: Why do so many Helm bugs come down to indentation, and what does nindent do about it?
answer_markdown: Helm is a text templating engine, not a Kubernetes-aware one. During rendering it has no model of Kubernetes objects at all — it produces a string, and only afterwards is that string parsed as YAML. Because indentation is semantically meaningful in YAML, a block injected at the wrong column does not produce a formatting nit, it produces a different data structure: a key that should have been nested becomes a sibling, or the document fails to parse entirely. nindent adds a newline and indents an injected block to a specified column, which is why you see toYaml piped into nindent whenever a whole subtree is inserted. The number must match the column the surrounding key's children require, and getting it wrong is exactly the bug you cannot see without rendering. The error message when it fails describes a line in generated output you never wrote, which is another reason to render deliberately.

prompt: A values file has replicaCont: 5 instead of replicaCount: 5. What happens, and how do you make this fail fast?
answer_markdown: Nothing fails. Values are just YAML with no schema by default, so the typo creates a new key that no template ever reads, and the chart renders successfully using the default replica count. There is no warning, and the symptom appears later as "my value had no effect." The fix is values.schema.json, which validates the merged values before rendering begins. The line that matters most is additionalProperties: false, because that is what turns an unrecognised key into an immediate error naming the key — without it, the schema only checks the keys you spelled correctly and a misspelling still slips through. The trade-off is real friction: every legitimate new value now requires a schema edit. On any chart used by more than a couple of people, that friction is much cheaper than the debugging it prevents.

prompt: Charts are packaged into versioned tarballs before deployment. A change is committed but production does not pick it up, and the chart version is identical everywhere. An integrity check comparing the published tarball to the build output tarball passes. What is going on?
answer_markdown: The tarball was packaged before the source edit, so the artefact no longer matches the source it claims to be built from. The chart version is the same in both places, so nothing looks wrong, and the change is genuinely present in Git — which is why this is so confusing to diagnose. The important part is why the integrity check cannot help: comparing the published tarball against the build output tarball compares two copies of the same stale artefact, so it passes while confirming only that the copy step worked faithfully. It says nothing about whether either copy matches the source. The general principle is to verify an artefact against its source, not against another artefact — which in practice means fingerprinting the source tree deterministically at package time, recording that fingerprint alongside the artefact, and re-deriving it from source to compare. Any check comparing two derived copies validates the copy, never the derivation.

prompt: Would you choose Helm or Kustomize, and why?
answer_markdown: It depends on the use case, and refusing to declare a universal winner is the correct answer. Helm fits distribution: publishing a chart for consumers whose requirements you cannot know requires conditionals, loops and versioned packages, and installing third-party software effectively requires Helm because that is how it is shipped. Kustomize fits your own services across environments you control, where differences are a handful of fields — its base is real, directly appliable YAML and overlays are structured patches, so there is no text-generation failure mode and no need to render to know what you will get. Helm's honest costs are that templating text to produce YAML is fragile, chart-version diffs are hard to read because you compare templates rather than outcomes, and deeply conditional charts become unpredictable. Kustomize's cost is that a patch targeting nothing silently no-ops, and it has no release history or rollback. Many teams use both: Kustomize for their own applications, Helm for vendor software, sometimes Kustomize patching Helm's rendered output to get structured edits over a chart they do not own.
